readings.title: A harvest box with flexible contents
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A cooperative sold weekly vegetable boxes. Customers liked local produce but complained that the same vegetables appeared too often. The main obstacle was boxes planned before the harvest was known. Weather changed which crops were ready, while advance lists gave buyers expectations the growers could not always meet. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a comparison of harvest records and complaints. Growers reviewed several weeks of crops and asked customers which substitutions they would accept. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated choice within groups was more useful than fixed lists. Buyers could plan meals when the box promised categories rather than particular vegetables. The group then introduced a flexible list published each harvest day. The cooperative offered a few swap choices and explained why local crops could vary. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: honest flexibility supports local supply. A reliable service need not pretend that weather and seasonal growth can be completely controlled. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in a harvest box with flexible contents, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Keeping produce cool at the market
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A weekend market sold berries from nearby farms. Fruit sometimes softened before noon despite having been picked that morning. The main obstacle was sun exposure at the busiest stalls. Farmers brought cool containers, but fruit sat on open tables while customers made their choices. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used temperature notes at different display points. Sellers measured conditions through the morning and compared covered and uncovered tables. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated shade protected quality during the waiting period. The largest difference came after the fruit left its container, not during the short journey to the market. The group then introduced smaller shaded displays with regular replacement. Sellers refilled tables from covered containers and told buyers how to keep fruit at home. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: freshness depends on each stage of handling. Careful growing can be lost if a brief display period is ignored. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in keeping produce cool at the market, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A school garden after summer
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A primary school planted herbs for science lessons. Most plants survived spring, but the garden looked neglected after the holiday. The main obstacle was no agreed responsibility during school closure. Teachers expected volunteers to help, yet nobody knew which days needed attention or how much water was appropriate. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a review of summer visits and plant conditions. The school compared the volunteer log with weather records and advice from experienced local gardeners. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated missed weeks mattered more than total visits. Several volunteers came on the same day while the garden remained unattended during a later dry period. The group then introduced a shared calendar and suitable plant choices. The school chose hardy plants and gave each helper a clear, limited task. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: education projects need a maintenance plan. The useful learning experience included caring for the garden between the enjoyable planting days. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in a school garden after summer, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Explaining food dates
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A food-sharing group collected unopened groceries. Volunteers noticed that usable items were sometimes discarded because date labels were misunderstood. The main obstacle was confusion between quality and safety dates. People treated every printed date alike although different labels called for different handling. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used guidance checked with food safety specialists. The group gathered examples and asked qualified advisers to explain the rules volunteers should follow. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated clear categories reduced uncertain decisions. Volunteers were more consistent when each label led to a specific, approved action. The group then introduced a short sorting guide and supervised training. The group kept its safety rules strict while avoiding needless waste where guidance allowed. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: good intentions require accurate information. Food sharing works best when volunteers understand both the opportunity to reduce waste and their duty to protect people. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in explaining food dates, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
A useful plan for local agriculture and food supply must take account of the people who will use it. An idea may look complete on paper and still create difficulties during an ordinary week. Organizers therefore tried the local food cooperation programme on a small scale and invited comments from users with different schedules. They recorded benefits as well as the time and resources needed to provide them. Some findings supported the original aim, while others suggested that the method should change. The group published both kinds of result instead of presenting the trial as a simple success or failure. This allowed residents to discuss the next step with a clearer understanding of its possible effects.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供考生自评，注意语义准确、逻辑关系及汉语通顺。
translation.referenceAnswer: 关于本地农业与食物供应的有用方案必须考虑实际使用它的人。一个想法在纸上看似完整，平常使用时却仍可能出现困难。因此，组织者小规模试行该服务，并邀请时间安排不同的使用者提出意见。他们既记录益处，也记录提供这些益处所需的时间和资源。有些发现支持最初目标，另一些则表明方法应当调整。团队同时公布两类结果，而没有把试行简单说成成功或失败。这让居民能更清楚地了解可能的影响，再讨论下一步。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the growers association about a community activity related to local agriculture and food supply. Explain how different people can participate, what should be recorded, and how the results should be shared.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the local food cooperation programme. People have noticed boxes planned before the harvest was known, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
